summary: Chronosphere is a public web tool that shows how any spot of the sky changes in NASA's SPHEREx images. Type a name or coordinates, or click the all-sky map, and the tool finds every SPHEREx exposure of that spot, lines them up and plays them like a little video, so that anything that moved or changed brightness stands out. From the same exposures it builds the spot's 102-band spectrum on the fly, measures the motion and the change in brightness, and says in plain sentences what the measurements show. It answers the challenge point by point: names or coordinates as input, image sequences over time, sums and differences of visits, a field of view you choose, Gaia and WISE overlays, coordinates in the URL, metadata and pixel flags, and an index designed to be refreshed automatically as new data arrive. It was tested on the five objects the challenge names; the motion it measures for Barnard's Star (10.4 arcseconds a year) and Epsilon Indi B (4.6) agrees with the catalogues. There is no server and nothing to install: the page reads NASA's open data directly in the browser, works on a phone, keeps what you have opened for use offline, and speaks six languages, so that many more people can help look.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Chronosphere lets anyone look at one spot of the sky through time. Search by name or by coordinates (decimal, sexagesimal, or pasted with their labels), or click the map of the whole sky in SPHEREx's 102 bands. The panel then shows the image sequence (one stacked image per visit, every single exposure, time as colour, differences between visits, each of the six detectors, a deep stack), the spectrum from 0.75 to 5 microns built on the fly with the bands of water, methane, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide, the brightness over time, the measured motion next to the catalogue value, Gaia DR3 and WISE sources laid over the image, and the metadata of every exposure including the pipeline's pixel flags by name. A guided tour of twelve steps begins with how Pluto was found and why Planet X is hard to see, then visits the five test objects of the challenge.

HOW IT WORKS

There is no server. A compact index of about 1.6 million public SPHEREx exposures tells the browser which files cover a position. The browser reads only the header and a small block of pixels of each file from NASA's open data (HTTP range requests: a few hundred kilobytes instead of 63 MB), aligns the blocks on one grid with each exposure's own astrometry, and computes stacks, differences, photometry and spectra on the device. A service worker keeps the page, the tour and every place already opened, so they work without a connection.

HOW IT WAS CHECKED

The browser's reader was compared with an independent Python implementation built on Astropy. Measured motion: Barnard's Star 10.4 arcseconds a year (catalogue 10.4), Epsilon Indi B 4.6 (catalogue 4.7), WISE 0855 7.0 (catalogue 8.2; it is faint and was detected in two visits only). Ordinary stars in the same images stay within 0.3 arcseconds. The pixel flags read in the browser are identical to Astropy's in every pixel tested.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Volunteers found most of the known brown dwarfs by comparing images taken at different times. Chronosphere brings that way of looking to SPHEREx for everyone: no installation, no login, phone and desktop, six languages (English, Turkish, Spanish, German, French, Polish). It links every spot to SIMBAD, WiseView, ESASky, the Legacy Survey and VizieR, so that a find can be checked elsewhere.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

HTML, CSS and JavaScript without a framework; Canvas; Aladin Lite (CDS) for the sky map; Service Worker and Cache API; GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions; Python with Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, PyVO and FastAPI for the reference implementation and the sky index.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

In SPHEREx data, stepping through time and building a spectrum are the same act, because every exposure sees a spot in a different colour; the tool shows both together. It states in plain words only what the measurements support, and says so when a star is too bright or too faint to judge. The sky map never shows a half-loaded picture, also on a slow connection.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED, AND THE LIMITS

New data must appear without changes to the code, so nothing about data releases is hard-coded. The tool does not identify asteroids or comets and claims no discovery. A dip at a molecule's wavelength is a hint, not a detection. Translations other than English and Turkish have not been read by native speakers.

USE OF AI TOOLS

AI tools (large language models used as coding and writing assistants) wrote most of the source code, the translations of the interface and drafts of the texts, under the team's direction. The results were checked against independent references: Astropy and the catalogues named above. Every image, measurement and spectrum the tool shows is computed from NASA data; none is AI-generated.

SOURCE CODE (GPL-3.0)

https://github.com/muhammetmucahitsoylu/chronosphere
